situation: Invited to a coworker's birthday party. Haven't responded to the invitation for a week.
thoughts_extracted: Everyone will think I'm awkward or strange if I say something dumb
People can tell when someone doesn't belong
I'm not good at social stuff
Everyone is staring at me and evaluating me
If I'm not entertaining or interesting, people will see me as less than
If I'm just myself and quiet, people will think I'm boring and won't want to talk to me
If people don't engage with me, it proves there's something fundamentally wrong with me
coherence_explanation: The therapist established a highly coherent thought-emotion chain. The situation (coworker's party invitation) leads to automatic thoughts ("Everyone will judge how awkward I am," "I won't know what to say," "People will think I'm weird," "I'll embarrass myself," core belief: "I'm fundamentally not worth people's time") which logically produce the emotions of anxiety, dread, and feeling inadequate/panicked. The therapist expertly traced surface-level worries down to the core belief about fundamental unworthiness, and the patient's emotional responses (stomach dropping, dread, anxiety) perfectly align with these cognitions about social judgment and rejection. The chain makes complete logical sense - fear of judgment and beliefs about being socially incompetent naturally produce anxiety and avoidance behaviors.

conceptualization.situation: Coworker invited patient to birthday party; patient has avoided responding for a week and feels dread when thinking about attending
thoughts: Everyone will think I'm awkward or strange if I say something dumb
People can tell when someone doesn't belong
I'm not good at social stuff
Everyone is staring at me and evaluating me
If I'm not entertaining or interesting, people will see me as less than
If I'm just myself and quiet, people will think I'm boring and won't want to talk to me
If people don't engage with me, it proves there's something fundamentally wrong with me
meaning_of_at: My worth depends on how entertaining, witty, or socially smooth I am
I am fundamentally not the kind of person people naturally gravitate toward
I don't belong in group social settings
Being quiet or not performing means I'm not good enough
People judge me harshly for social missteps the way I judge myself
behaviors: Avoids responding to the party invite
Engages in safety behaviors (rehearsing conversations mentally)
Checks the invite to see who's attending
Performs or tries to appear entertaining in group settings (internally, through worry)
One-on-one conversations are natural, but withdraws in groups

conversation: Therapist: How are you?

Patient: Hey, I'm doing okay, thanks for asking! Just been a bit in my head lately if I'm being honest. Work's been fine, it's just... there's this thing I've been stressing about and I keep putting it off, which honestly makes it worse lol.

Therapist: I appreciate you sharing that with me. It sounds like you're experiencing some stress and procrastination around something specific. Before we dive deeper, I'd like to understand this better: What's the thing that's been on your mind that you've been putting off? And when you think about it, what feeling comes up first—is it worry, dread, overwhelm, or something else?

Patient: Yeah, so it's kind of silly actually... my coworker invited me to their birthday party and I just haven't responded. It's been like a week now lol. 

And honestly? When I think about going, I just feel this sense of dread, like my stomach drops. I know I should just say yes or no but every time I think about it I get anxious. It's stupid because they seem nice enough, but I just... I dunno, I keep imagining how awkward it's gonna be if I go.

Therapist: It's definitely not silly—what you're describing is really common, and I appreciate you being honest about it. So let me make sure I'm understanding: when you imagine going to this party, you get anxious and picture it being awkward. That physical sensation—the stomach drop—that's your body's way of telling you something feels threatening. 

Before we go further, I want to understand what specifically feels awkward or threatening to you about the party. When you imagine yourself there, what's the scene that plays in your head? What do you see yourself doing or not doing that feels uncomfortable?

Patient: Okay so like... I picture myself standing there and just not knowing what to say to people, you know? Like everyone's gonna be talking and laughing and I'm just gonna be awkwardly standing there trying to think of something that doesn't sound weird.

And then I start thinking like... what if I say something dumb? Or what if there's an awkward silence and everyone just stares at me? I keep running through conversations in my head trying to figure out what would sound normal, but nothing feels right.

I guess I'm also worried about who else will be there. Like, what if it's all people who know each other really well and I'm just the odd one out? I'd probably just want to leave early anyway... honestly I've been looking at the invite trying to see who's going lol.

It's just like... I feel like people are gonna see how weird I am or something. That I don't really belong there.

Therapist: Okay, I'm hearing something really important here. You're having multiple anxious thoughts layered on top of each other—worrying about saying something wrong, imagining people staring at you, fearing you'll be left out, and underneath all of that is this deeper belief that you're "weird" and don't belong. That's a lot to carry in your head at once, and no wonder your stomach drops when you think about it. 

Let me ask you something: When you imagine saying something "dumb," what specifically are you afraid will happen? Like, if you stumbled over your words or made a joke that didn't land—what's the worst outcome you're picturing? Because I want to understand what you think people will do or think about you if that happens.

Patient: Ugh, okay so like... if I say something dumb, I'm imagining people will just kinda judge me, you know? Like they'll think I'm awkward or strange. And then I'll be that person—the weird coworker who doesn't fit in.

I guess the worst case is just... everyone will see that I'm not good at this social stuff. Like they'll realize I'm just kinda incompetent when it comes to talking to people. And then it'll be awkward the next time I see them at work, and they'll remember that I was the awkward one at the party.

Honestly? I think people just naturally pick up on those kinds of things about you, you know? Like they can tell when someone doesn't belong or when someone's different. And I feel like that's just... kinda who I am in social situations. I'm just not great at it, and people sense that.

*pauses*

Like even right now I'm probably coming across as weird lol. Does that make sense or am I just overthinking this?

Therapist: You're not coming across as weird at all—you're being really thoughtful and self-aware, actually. And what you've just described makes complete sense. I want to highlight something important I'm noticing: you've got this core belief that "I'm just not good at social stuff" and "people can sense when I don't belong," and then everything else—the worry about saying something dumb, imagining people judging you, avoiding the party—that all stems from that one belief. It's like your mind is using that belief as a lens to interpret everything, including right now in this conversation.

Here's what I'm curious about: where did that belief come from? Like, can you think back to experiences that made you feel like you're socially incompetent or that you don't belong? Because I want to understand if this belief is based on actual evidence, or if it's something your anxious mind has convinced you is true.

Patient: *thinks for a moment*

Hmm, that's a good question actually. Like... I don't know if there's one specific thing, you know? It's more like a feeling I've had for a while. I guess in high school I wasn't like the super social kid—I had a few close friends but I wasn't in the popular group or anything.

And now that I think about it, there have been times where I've said something and people didn't laugh or seemed confused, and I was like "oh great, they think I'm weird." But like... when I really think about it, I can't actually point to a time where someone told me I don't belong or anything. 

*pauses*

Actually, I remember at my last job there was this work lunch and I went, and I felt anxious the whole time. But looking back... people actually seemed fine with me being there? My coworker even invited me to stuff after that. So like... I don't know. Maybe I'm just assuming people think I'm weird without actually having proof they do?

It's weird because I can have conversations with people one-on-one just fine. But in group settings something shifts in my head and I'm like convinced everyone's judging me. Even though I can't really point to why I think that.

Therapist: This is a really important realization you're having right now. You're noticing something crucial: there's a gap between what you *feel* (that everyone's judging you) and what you can actually *prove* happened. That gap is where the anxiety lives.

Here's what I'm seeing: Your mind is essentially treating your anxiety—that stomach drop feeling, the worry—as *evidence* that you don't belong. It feels so real and so certain that you assume it must be true. But you just gave me examples showing that's not necessarily the case. At your last job, people actually seemed fine with you, yet you *felt* judged. So the feeling and the reality didn't match up, right?

What if we looked at this differently: What if that anxious feeling in group settings isn't actually telling you the truth about what people think of you? What if it's just your brain's threat detection system working overtime—like a smoke detector that's too sensitive and going off when there's no fire?

Here's what I want to explore with you: When you're one-on-one with someone, what's different in your head? Why does the anxiety shift in group settings?

Patient: *nods slowly*

Oh man, yeah... when I'm talking to someone one-on-one I'm like totally fine. I can just be myself, ask them about their day, whatever. It feels natural.

But in a group? It's like... I dunno, there's so many eyes on me? Or I feel like there are anyway. Like I have to perform or something. And if I'm not saying something clever or funny, then I'm just... taking up space? And everyone can see that I'm just standing there being quiet, which then makes me feel like they're noticing how awkward I am.

*pauses*

Which like... now that I'm saying it out loud, that doesn't really make sense does it? People aren't just staring at me waiting for me to entertain them. They're talking to each other, doing their own thing. But in my head it feels like all the attention is on me and if I mess up, everyone will see it.

It's like the group setting somehow makes me feel like I'm being evaluated or something. Like I have to prove I'm worth being there. One-on-one there's no evaluation—it's just a conversation.

Do you think that's like... a normal thing people feel or is that just me being weird about it?

Therapist: You're definitely not alone in this—what you're describing is actually really common, especially for people with social anxiety. But here's what I want to focus on: you've just identified something powerful. You feel like you're being *evaluated* in group settings, like you need to *prove* you belong. That's the core anxiety driving everything—it's not really about saying something dumb, it's about feeling like you're on trial.

So here's my next question: When you imagine being at this party and standing quietly, what specifically do you think people are evaluating you *for*? Like, what would make you "pass" that evaluation in your mind? What would it mean to be worth being there?

Patient: *sits with that for a second*

Wow, okay... that's hitting different. Like, I guess I'd need to be like... entertaining? Or at least saying things that make sense and don't make people uncomfortable. Like I'd need to prove I'm someone worth talking to, you know?

But like... *laughs a little* when I say that out loud, it sounds exhausting. Like I'm putting all this pressure on myself to be a certain way just to like... deserve to be at a birthday party for a coworker.

*pauses*

And honestly? I think part of me believes that if I'm not being entertaining or interesting, then people naturally just... see me as less than or something. Like my value depends on how witty I am or how smooth I am socially. If I'm just being normal or quiet, then I'm like... boring? Not good enough?

Which is kinda messed up when I think about it, because I don't judge other people like that at all. Like at work, I don't think "oh that person's quiet so they're not worth knowing." I just... think they're fine. But I don't extend that same thing to myself.

*looks down*

Why do I do that?

Therapist: That's a really profound observation you just made—and I want you to sit with that insight for a moment because it's huge. You just noticed something most people miss: you have a double standard. You're compassionate and accepting of others when they're quiet or not "performing," but you're harsh and demanding with yourself. You believe you need to earn your place through entertainment, but you don't think others need to do that.

That gap right there? That's where we can work. The "why" is often rooted in beliefs you picked up somewhere—maybe from family, school, or just the world telling you that your worth is tied to what you do or how you perform. But here's what matters: you're aware of it now.

Before we go deeper into the "why," I want to ask: When you sit with the idea of just... going to this party and being *normal*—not entertaining, just present, maybe quiet, maybe contributing when you feel like it—what comes up for you? What's the fear there?

Patient: *takes a breath*

Okay so like... if I just go and be normal and quiet, the fear is that people will just... not care? Or worse, they'll notice I'm not trying and think "oh, she's boring" or "why is she even here?"

But also there's like this other fear underneath that—if I go and nobody really engages with me, or if I'm just kinda in the background, then that'll prove that I don't actually belong there. Like it will confirm what I already believe about myself.

*voice gets quieter*

It's like... I'm scared that if I'm just myself and that's not enough to make people want to talk to me, then that means there's something actually wrong with me. Not just in that moment, but like... fundamentally. That I'm just not the kind of person people naturally gravitate toward.

*pauses*

And I guess that's why I keep avoiding responding to the invite, right? Because as long as I don't go, I don't have to find out if that's true. I can keep telling myself "oh it would've been awkward anyway" instead of actually testing whether people would've been cool with me being there.

Does that make sense?

Therapist: That makes complete sense, and what you've just articulated is really the heart of it. You're avoiding the party not because it will definitely be awkward—it's because you're afraid of finding out that your deepest fear might be true: that you're fundamentally not worth people's time or connection. So avoidance feels safer than taking that risk.

But here's what I want you to notice: you've actually already done something really brave in this conversation. You've been yourself—quiet sometimes, thoughtful, a bit self-critical—and I'm still here, still engaged, still genuinely interested in understanding you. Not because you entertained me or performed, but because you're being real. That already challenges the belief you're holding.

So here's my challenge for you: What if the fear itself—that deep belief that you're fundamentally not worth it—what if that's the thing we need to examine? Not whether you should go to the party, but whether that core belief is actually true or if it's something your anxiety has convinced you of. Because right now, you're making major life decisions based on a belief you can't actually prove, and your anxiety is protecting that belief by keeping you away from evidence that might disprove it.

What would it feel like to test that belief instead of hiding from it?

Patient: *long pause*

Honestly? It feels terrifying. Like... if I go to this party and actually try—like actually show up and be myself—and people still don't engage or whatever, then I'd have to face that maybe I was right all along. That would be worse than just avoiding it, you know?

But also... *hesitates* ...I'm realizing that's not really fair logic either. Like, one party where maybe one interaction doesn't go great doesn't prove I'm fundamentally unworthy. I know that logically. But it *feels* like it would.

*rubs face*

And I guess the thing is... I've been avoiding this invite for a week and I don't actually feel better. I just feel more anxious about it. Like the dread's still there, it's just been building.

*quietly*

What if I went and nothing catastrophic happened? Like... what if people were just... normal to me? Not mean, not rejecting, just... normal? Would that change how I see myself or would I just find another reason to think I don't belong?

I don't know if I'm ready to do that yet though. Like intellectually I get it, but actually walking in there feeling like this... I don't know if I can.

Therapist: You've done something really important here—you've identified the exact cycle keeping you stuck. The avoidance isn't protecting you; it's feeding the anxiety and the belief. That takes courage to see. Here's what I want you to know: you don't need to feel ready to do this. Anxiety never gives you permission—it just creates more doubt. What matters is whether you're willing to try, even while feeling scared. 

Before we talk about the party, I want to give you something concrete to work with. This week, could you challenge one small assumption? Pick one social interaction—maybe with your coworker, or literally anyone—and notice what actually happens versus what you predicted would happen. Don't perform or try hard. Just observe the gap between your fear and reality. That data matters.

And about the party—we don't have to decide today. But what if we looked at it not as a pass/fail test of your worth, but as an experiment? You go, you're yourself, and you simply notice what happens without judging it as proof of anything. Can you sit with that idea?

Patient: *nods slowly*

Yeah, okay... I can try that. The small interaction thing makes sense. Like, just notice without all the judgment attached to it. That feels less overwhelming than "prove you belong at the party."

*pauses*

And I guess... I could respond to the invite this week? Like not commit to going necessarily, but just actually respond instead of leaving it hanging. That's like a small step, right? Because leaving it unanswered is kind of its own form of avoiding.

*voice gets a bit steadier*

I think what you said about the anxiety never giving permission—that hit different. Like I've been waiting to feel confident or ready, but maybe that's not how it works. Maybe I just have to do it scared.

*hesitates*

But like... if I do go, and I'm there feeling anxious the whole time, how do I not just spiral and convince myself everyone can see how nervous I am?

That's the part I'm still stuck on. Like I can intellectually get the belief stuff, but when I'm actually *in* it, in my body with the racing heart and everything... how do I manage that part?

Therapist: That's exactly the right question—and honestly, it shows you're thinking practically. Here's the truth: you won't make the anxiety disappear before you go. But we can work on how you relate to it *while* you're there. That's different.

When your heart races or you feel nervous, that's just a physical sensation—it's not a sign you're failing or that people can see it like a neon sign. Most of what you imagine people seeing, they actually can't. And here's the key: people are usually too focused on their own stuff to be analyzing your anxiety level.

What we can do is build some specific tools for when you're there: grounding techniques to help you stay present instead of spiraling, ways to redirect your attention when anxiety spikes, and a realistic plan for what you'll actually do (not perform, just... be). 

But here's what I want to explore first: When you imagine yourself at the party feeling anxious, what's the thought that usually comes next? Like, your heart races and then your brain tells you... what? That's where we can interrupt the spiral before it starts.

This is our work for next time we talk—I want you to really notice those moments this week when anxiety shows up in a social situation. What's the automatic thought? Because once we identify that, we have something concrete to work with. Sound good?

Patient: *nods*

Yeah, that makes sense. So like... notice the physical stuff, then notice what my brain is telling me right now. Got it.

*thinks*

I guess when my heart races, the thought is usually like "everyone can tell I'm nervous" or "I'm obviously uncomfortable and that makes me weird." And then from there it spirals into like "they're judging me right now" and "I need to leave."

*pauses*

So this week I'll like... pay attention to those moments. When the anxiety shows up, what am I actually *thinking* versus what's real. And I'll respond to the invite—like actually send a message even if I'm not 100% sure yet.

*small smile*

And maybe try one normal interaction and just observe without the whole performance pressure thing.

Does that sound like a decent plan? Because honestly I'm feeling like... a little less stuck than I did at the start of this conversation. Not like magically fixed or anything, but like at least there's something to actually *do* instead of just avoid.

Therapist: That's exactly the right plan, and I'm genuinely impressed by the work you've done here today. You went from "I haven't responded to this invite" to identifying the core belief driving everything, recognizing the avoidance cycle, and committing to concrete steps. That's real progress.

Here's what I want you to remember this week: You're not trying to fix yourself or prove anything. You're just gathering information. Notice the thoughts, notice what actually happens, respond to that invite. Small steps. And when the anxiety tells you that you can't do this or that you're too weird—you remember this conversation and the gap you already found between what you fear and what's actually true.

We'll pick this up next time and build on what you've learned. You've got this, and I'm here to help you work through it. How are you feeling about starting this week?

situation: Made a minor error in a presentation to the team. Manager said 'we can discuss this later.'
thoughts_extracted: I was never cut out for this job
I'm a failure as a person
My manager is disappointed in me
I'm not actually as capable as people think I am
coherence_explanation: The therapist established a coherent chain: Situation (minor mistake in presentation + manager's comment "we can discuss this later") → Automatic Thoughts ("I'm going to get fired," "Everyone thinks I'm incompetent," "I was never cut out for this job," "I don't belong here," "I'm a failure as a person," "My manager is disappointed in me," "I'm not actually as capable as people think I am") → Emotions (terror, dread, anxiety, fear of being found out, shame, exhaustion). This chain is highly logical - catastrophic thoughts about job security and competence naturally lead to feelings of terror, dread, and shame. The therapist also effectively traced these patterns back to childhood experiences of conditional approval based on performance.

Love and approval are conditional on perfect performance

Mistakes mean I'm a failure as a person, not just that I failed at a task

Checking job postings as an escape plan

conversation: Therapist: How are you?

Patient: Hey, I'm doing alright I guess. Just been a bit in my head, you know? Had this thing happen at work earlier and I can't really stop thinking about it. One of those days where you replay stuff over and over.

Therapist: I appreciate you sharing that. It sounds like something from work is weighing on your mind right now. Before we dive deeper, I want to understand what you're experiencing better. When you say you keep replaying it over and over—what specifically about that situation feels most distressing to you? Is it something someone said, something you did, or more about the outcome?

Patient: Yeah, so I messed up during this presentation to the team—like nothing huge, just a minor error. But my manager was like "we can discuss this later" and honestly? That killed me. 

Now I'm just spiraling. Like, everyone definitely thinks I'm incompetent now. I keep imagining the conversation later and I'm genuinely terrified about what's gonna happen. Part of me is even looking at other job postings because I feel like... I don't know, like maybe this is it for me here. 

It's stupid because logically I know it was a small thing, but it feels massive right now.

Therapist: I hear you—and it's not stupid at all. There's actually a lot happening here that we should unpack together. You're recognizing something really important: logically you know it was minor, but emotionally it feels catastrophic. That gap is exactly what we need to explore.

Let me ask you this: when your manager said "we can discuss this later," what went through your mind in that moment? Not the spiraling that came after, but right then—what was the very first thought that hit you?

Patient: Oh man, okay so... the immediate thought was like "I'm gonna get fired." Just like that. Super dramatic, right?

And then it just snowballed from there. Like, if I'm getting fired, then obviously everyone thinks I'm incompetent. And if that's true, then honestly... this just proves I was never really cut out for this job in the first place. Like maybe I'm not good enough, you know?

And I know how that sounds—one small mistake doesn't mean all that. But it's like my brain just took it and ran with it to the worst possible place. Everything feels like evidence that I don't belong here or something.

Therapist: You've just shown me something really important—and I want to acknowledge that first. You can see the pattern: a small mistake → "I'm getting fired" → "everyone thinks I'm incompetent" → "I was never cut out for this" → "I don't belong here." That's classic catastrophic thinking, and the fact that you can recognize it's happening is actually a huge strength.

Here's what I'm curious about: when you say "I don't belong here"—that feeling seems deeper than just this one presentation. Has this feeling of not being good enough shown up in other areas of your life, or is this something specific to work? And when you imagine that conversation with your manager later, what's the absolute worst thing you're afraid they'll say or do?

Patient: Honestly? Yeah, it shows up everywhere. Like, I feel this way a lot—like I'm somehow fooling people, you know? At work, with friends sometimes... there's always this underlying thing where I'm waiting to be found out. Like I'm not actually as capable as people think I am.

As for the conversation with my manager... I think the worst case is they're just disappointed. Like, not angry, just... let down. Like they realize I'm not who they thought I was. That I can't handle the responsibility they gave me. That I'm just fundamentally not cut out for it.

And then what? I'd have to find another job where I'd probably mess up eventually too, because clearly I'm the problem, not the situation.

I've actually been staying late at work trying to like, overcompensate or something. Hoping if I just work harder, they'll overlook the mistake or remember I'm actually decent at my job. But it's exhausting, man. And I keep checking those job postings even though I don't really want to leave.

Therapist: I'm really glad you're being this honest with me, because what you're describing goes beyond this one presentation—this is a deeper pattern where you've internalized the belief that you're fundamentally "not enough," and now you're constantly bracing for people to discover that. That's exhausting, and I can see why you're staying late and checking job postings even when you don't want to leave. You're trying to escape the feeling by working harder or planning an escape route, but neither actually addresses what's driving the anxiety.

Here's what I want to understand: When you imagine your manager being disappointed in you, what does that say about *you* as a person? Like, if they realize you made a mistake or have limitations—what does that mean you actually are? And I'm curious—where do you think this belief that you're not good enough originally came from? Was there something early on that taught you that your worth depended on being flawless or exceeding expectations?

Patient: Oof, okay that's a heavy question. 

So like, if my manager is disappointed... it means I'm a failure. Like, not just that I failed at that task, but that *I'm* a failure as a person. That I don't have what it takes. It's wild how fast my brain goes there.

And honestly? I think a lot of it comes from growing up. My parents were never like, explicitly harsh or anything, but there was always this vibe that mistakes weren't really... acceptable? Like, my older sibling was the golden child—always did everything right, got the grades, made the right choices. And I was always compared to that, you know? It felt like love and approval were tied to performance. Like if I wasn't excelling, I was letting everyone down.

So I think I internalized this thing where being good enough means being *perfect*. Like, anything less than that is basically worthless. And now at work, even one small mistake feels like proof that I don't deserve to be there.

The crazy part is I know that's not how normal people think about mistakes. But knowing it and actually believing something different are two totally different things.

Therapist: You've just connected something really crucial—and I want you to sit with this for a moment. You grew up learning that love, approval, and your worth were conditional on performance and perfection. So now, your brain has built this equation: mistakes = I'm not good enough = I don't deserve to be here. And when your manager said "we'll discuss this later," it triggered all of that old programming.

Here's the thing though—you're absolutely right that knowing something intellectually and truly believing it are different. But we can work on that gap. Right now, I want to ask: What if making one small mistake doesn't actually prove anything about your fundamental worth or capability? What if, instead, it just proves you're human? Can you imagine—just for a second—holding that as true? What comes up for you?

Also, I'm curious: when your manager eventually has that conversation with you, what do you think might actually happen versus what your anxiety is predicting?

Patient: Ugh, when you put it that way... intellectually I can see it. Like yeah, everyone makes mistakes. That's just being human. But when I try to actually *feel* that as true about myself? It's hard, man. There's this resistance. Like my brain is like "yeah but YOU'RE different, you need to be better."

And I guess what comes up is... fear? Like, if I accept that it's okay to make mistakes, does that mean I'll just keep making them? Does that mean I'm giving myself permission to be mediocre? It feels safer somehow to believe I need to be perfect, because at least then I'm... trying, you know?

As for the actual conversation... logically, I think my manager probably just wants to clarify what happened and maybe talk through how to handle it better next time. Like, a normal work conversation. They probably won't fire me. They might not even be that upset.

But my brain keeps going "yeah but what if they ARE upset, what if they've been waiting for a reason to let you go" and that feeling drowns out the logical part.

I know the actual outcome will probably be... fine. Maybe even constructive. But right now I can't shake this sense of dread about it. Like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop.

Therapist: You've identified something really important: you're confusing acceptance of your humanity with giving up or becoming mediocre. That's a core belief we need to challenge. The truth is—perfection isn't what made you competent; your actual skills, effort, and growth did. And those don't disappear when you accept that mistakes are part of being human.

Here's what I want you to notice: your brain is using anxiety as a *motivator*. It thinks "if I'm anxious and terrified, I'll be careful and won't mess up." But what's actually happening? The anxiety is exhausting you, making you ruminate, and it's not preventing mistakes—it's just making you miserable. That's the pattern we're going to work on breaking.

For now, I want you to try something: when that dread comes up before your conversation, pause and ask yourself, "What's the evidence that my manager wants to fire me?" versus "What's the evidence this might be a normal, constructive conversation?" Don't try to force belief—just notice what's actually true. Can you do that?

Patient: Yeah, okay... I can try that. When I actually think about it—like, real evidence—there's nothing that says they want to fire me. They've always been supportive.
